pieces.title: Wake Up Somewhere Else
pieces.dek: Twenty overnight trains, ferries and coaches on five continents, timed from evening departure to morning arrival, with how much of the next day each one really gives you.
pieces.design: Red Hat Display, Literata, Red Hat Mono; night-to-dawn gradient hero, linen paper, teal/rose-madder/ochre by mode; 24-hour arc dial, night-bar chart, connection-chain route cards.
pieces.brief:
The Overnight Geography Directory
Research question: Where can you travel overnight, wake up somewhere genuinely different, and still have a useful amount of time to explore before returning?
Rather than listing sleeper trains alone, this guide investigates the geography of overnight travel: night trains, late ferries, overnight coaches, and useful early-morning arrivals.
Proposed contents
- 20 origin–destination connections.
- Departure and arrival times, journey duration, and arrival-day usefulness.
- Available accommodation types or seating arrangements.
- Connections to local transit upon arrival.
- Seasonal operation and booking constraints.
- A distinction between journeys that save hotel costs and those that primarily save daytime travel.
Interactive element: A route planner that filters by mode, overnight duration, arrival time, and whether the destination offers a full usable day. Use original HTML route cards rather than embedded map imagery.
Sources to start from: Verify current schedules, seasonal services, and booking conditions when researching each route.
Finish line: 20 verified routes, five useful route comparisons, and a filterable directory that identifies the strongest options for maximizing time at the destination.

pieces.title: The Ghosts of Empires
pieces.dek: Seventeen arrangements left by empires, from a border in the Hindu Kush to a currency peg in West Africa, traced from the original decision to what they still decide today.
pieces.design: Marcellus, Gentium Book Plus, Noto Sans Mono; survey-vellum, plum ink over sepia ghost lines; palimpsest hero, afterlife bar chart, trace-what-survived ledgers.
pieces.brief:
The Ghosts of Empires
Create an interactive HTML guide tracing overlooked colonial and imperial arrangements that continue to shape the modern world.
Investigate specific inherited borders, legal systems, property rules, infrastructure networks, language policies, resource concessions, and administrative categories.
For each case, trace the original decision through historical turning points to its documented present-day consequences.
Explain what survived independence, what changed, and who benefited or suffered, without reducing complex histories to simplistic explanations.
Include interactive timelines and original schematic maps showing how historical arrangements persist.
Use original HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and SVG; no external images or copyrighted visual assets.

pieces.title: The Secret Histories of Ordinary Life
pieces.dek: Ten everyday systems, from house numbers and surnames to plugs and price tags, traced from what came before to who fixed them and what they quietly changed.
pieces.design: Big Shoulders Display, Source Serif 4, IBM Plex Mono; enamel street-sign cobalt on plaster wall, signal red, brass; number-plate index, before/after panels, lane timeline.
pieces.brief:
The Secret Histories of Ordinary Life
Create an interactive HTML guide uncovering the surprising histories behind ordinary things such as passports, hotel keys, time zones, barcodes, shipping containers, electrical plugs, and street addresses.
Explain what existed before each system, why it emerged, who standardized it, and how it changed society.
Explore the political, commercial, technological, and cultural consequences hidden behind seemingly mundane conventions.
Prioritize stories that fundamentally change how readers understand everyday life, not merely amusing invention trivia.
Build an interactive atlas with historical timelines, before-and-after comparisons, and “still with us” explanations.
Use original HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and SVG; no external images or copyrighted visual assets.

pieces.title: Reaching the Water
pieces.dek: Twenty harbour, river, lake and sea cities: what stands between each one and its water, how it got there, what was removed, and a scorecard comparing public access and how well each waterfront is woven into the city.
pieces.design: Vollkorn with Commissioner; nautical-chart buff land, depth-tint blues, chart magenta; chart hero with cartouche, city-to-water cross-section strips, pip scores, depth-tinted scorecard.
pieces.brief:
The Urban Waterfront Access Atlas
Research question: Which cities make their waterfronts part of ordinary urban life, and which effectively separate the city from the water?
This is a way to explore your interest in coastal cities, waterfront architecture, overlooked luxury districts, and places where geography shapes everyday life.
Proposed contents
- 20 waterfront cities, including riverfront, harbor, lakefront, and seafront examples.
- Public access to the water and continuity of walking routes.
- Ferries, promenades, beaches, waterfront markets, and public transport.
- The relationship between residential neighborhoods, commercial districts, and the waterfront.
- Barriers such as highways, port facilities, steep terrain, or private developments.
- A short profile of what makes each waterfront distinctive.
Interactive element: A filterable atlas organized by waterfront type, public accessibility, and urban integration. Include original CSS-based access diagrams showing how the built environment connects—or fails to connect—to the water.
Sources to start from: Use verified municipal planning information and public-access information during research.
Finish line: 20 cities classified into four waterfront types, plus a comparative scorecard for public access and urban integration.

pieces.title: The Decisions That Accidentally Built Our World
pieces.dek: Seventeen treaties, standards and committee choices, from Tordesillas to the 160-character text, with who made each one, what they were trying to do, and what followed that nobody planned.
pieces.design: Bodoni Moda, Newsreader, Archivo Narrow; conference-baize green, cool minute-paper, sealing-wax red, brass; top-down table hero, agenda items with Resolved blocks, consequence chains, myth/record boxes.
pieces.brief:
The Decisions That Accidentally Built Our World
Create an interactive HTML guide to obscure decisions, treaties, technical standards, and bureaucratic choices that unexpectedly shaped the modern world.
Investigate how small groups or individual officials made decisions with lasting consequences for borders, commerce, infrastructure, communication, or identity.
For each case, explain the original problem, decision-makers, alternatives, motivations, and long-term effects.
Distinguish unintended consequences from deliberate outcomes and later historical myths.
Include interactive timelines, consequence chains, and clearly labeled counterfactual scenarios.
Focus on overlooked turning points that help explain why today's world works the way it does.
Use original HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and SVG; no external images or copyrighted visual assets.

pieces.title: Houses That Tell You Who Lived There
pieces.dek: Fifteen landmark European houses built for rich clients between 1894 and 1959, and what each plan, material and doorway reveals about how its owners wanted to live.
pieces.design: Josefin Sans, Cardo, Inconsolata; drafting-grid paper, graphite, ochre/verdigris/brick use-codes; title-block hero of floor stacks, plates with section keys, privacy–display scatter.
pieces.brief:
Houses That Tell You Who Lived There
A building-by-building guide to landmark European houses and apartment buildings designed for wealthy clients, and what each one says about how its owners wanted to live. Where The Secret Geography of European Luxury maps districts, this one goes inside single buildings: the commission, the architect, the plan, the materials, and how the design signalled status in its day.
Include: 15 buildings from about 1890 to the present, favouring ones that are now museums, heritage-listed or thoroughly documented (the level of Villa Tugendhat, Palais Stoclet or Casa Malaparte). Simple drawn plans or sections where they help. For each house, a short note on what it would tell a novelist about a character who lived there.
Avoid: current private residents, property prices, live listings.
Look: an architectural monograph or plan book.
Finish line: 15 building profiles, a timeline of styles, and a comparison matrix of how each house balances privacy against display.

pieces.title: The Things Countries Actually Wrote Down
pieces.dek: Fifty-one clauses from constitutions and founding laws, quoted in their own words, with what they meant, what became of them, and the famous lines that were never written at all.
pieces.design: EB Garamond, Inria Sans, Sometype Mono; statute-paper white, iron-gall ink, legal pink tape; tied-bundle hero, side-noted clauses, status tabs, side-by-side concordance.
pieces.brief:
The Things Countries Actually Wrote Down
Create a self-contained interactive HTML guide exploring the most astonishing, consequential, or overlooked provisions in countries’ constitutions, foundational laws, declarations, and official records.
Find authentic passages involving unusual rights, citizen duties, state powers, historical compromises, and unexpected national commitments.
For each, provide the exact wording, country, document, date, legal status, historical context, and real-world implications.
Distinguish current law from repealed provisions, proposals, mistranslations, and misleading quotations.
Build a searchable explorer with filters by country, subject, era, and legal status, plus side-by-side comparisons.
Prioritize discoveries that reveal something profound or surprising about a country's history or political system.
Use original HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and SVG; no external images or copyrighted visual assets.

pieces.title: The Geography of Disappearing Wealth
pieces.dek: A dossier on six cities where diamonds, watches and art are legitimately traded, stored and checked, and on what documented cases show about how stolen valuables are traced across borders.
pieces.design: Fraunces, PT Serif, Space Mono; diamond-parcel paper, lining ultramarine, trace teal, ochre; opened-parcel hero, object/paper track diagram, sourced network map, case tabs.
pieces.brief:
The Geography of Disappearing Wealth
Research question: How do luxury goods, money, and ownership move between legitimate commercial centers, and what can those networks tell us about the geography of modern crime?
This is the most direct extension of your Pink Panthers research. The focus is not on reconstructing how to commit a theft, but on the legitimate industries and cross-border relationships surrounding valuable objects.
Proposed contents
- A geographic dossier covering Antwerp, Belgrade, Milan, Monaco, Geneva, and London.
- The roles of jewelers, gem laboratories, auction houses, dealers, and luxury resale businesses.
- The difference between an object's physical movement and its documented ownership.
- Documented cases illustrating how investigators trace stolen goods.
- A glossary of trade terminology and an evidence table separating established facts from reporting and speculation.
Visual element: An interactive network map linking cities, institutions, industries, and documented cases. Each connection should explain what is established and cite its source.
Sources to start with: OCCRP, INTERPOL's stolen works of art database, and the New Yorker's reporting on the Pink Panthers. The latter is particularly useful for understanding how the investigation crossed national borders and why the group's organization remained uncertain. 
Finish line: Six city profiles, 15–20 documented entities or institutions, a sourced relationship map, and five case studies. Label allegations carefully and avoid implying that ordinary businesses are involved in crime without evidence.
Review: yes

pieces.title: Signal Check
pieces.dek: A newsroom field manual for verifying radio broadcasts, live feeds and audio recordings while a big story is breaking, with a one-page verification flowchart and six case files.
pieces.design: Schibsted Grotesk, Brygada 1918, Fragment Mono; spectrogram indigo-to-lime (viridis) on teleprinter ivory; waterfall hero with tuning dial, log-sheet procedures, signal-path flowchart.
pieces.brief:
Radio Intelligence & Broadcast Verification Guide
The Concept: A technical field manual for verifying live news, eyewitness feeds, and radio broadcasts during major geopolitical events. Move beyond standard social media OSINT to focus on audio-visual signal verification and newsroom-grade source assessment.
Key Content: Cross-referencing shortwave/digital radio feeds, verifying live audio broadcasts (e.g., evaluating live coverage from international news outlets), audio spectrum analysis, verifying timestamps against daylight/timezones, and cross-checking eyewitness statements with local emergency services.
Finish Line: A clean, single-page verification flowchart plus a case study examining a breaking live news broadcast and how to spot synthetic audio or misattributed recordings.

pieces.title: The Botanical Drinks Laboratory
pieces.dek: A working reference for building complex, low-sugar drinks from herbs, spices and peel: what twelve botanicals contribute, how extraction changes them, and three prototype recipes to start from.
pieces.design: IM Fell English, Hanken Grotesk, Cutive Mono; herbarium-board grey-green, leaf green, kraft label slips; mounted-specimen hero, compound range strips, pairing matrix, tasting radar.
pieces.brief:
The Botanical Drinks Laboratory
Research question: How can you create complex, savory, low-sugar drinks using herbs, spices, citrus, and other botanicals?
This is a practical guide to flavor experimentation, drawing on your interest in infusions and drinks that aren't dominated by sweetness.
Proposed contents
- A flavor reference for coriander seed, rosemary, mint, citrus peel, ginger, black pepper, and other botanicals.
- Water-based infusions versus oil- or alcohol-based extraction.
- How steeping time, temperature, and ingredient size influence extraction.
- Three prototype directions: a bitter-citrus spritz base, a savory herbal tonic, and a ginger-spice concentrate.
- A tasting sheet for aroma, bitterness, acidity, body, and finish.
- Ingredient cost per serving and batch scaling.
Visual element: A botanical pairing matrix. Select a base ingredient and a desired flavor profile to reveal promising combinations and suggested starting ratios.
Sources to start with: Harold McGee's Curious Cook for food chemistry, NIST Chemistry WebBook for reference data on individual compounds, and USDA FoodData Central for ingredient composition.
Finish line: A 12-ingredient reference table and three small-batch recipes with a standardized tasting worksheet. Keep any room-temperature storage claims out of scope unless the preservation process has been validated.

pieces.title: Chain of Custody
pieces.dek: How a vote becomes a certified result, stage by stage: the American system that goes to the polls on 3 November, ten other democracies, and the times the chain broke.
pieces.design: Libre Franklin, Crimson Pro, Overpass Mono; ballot-buff, indelible-ink violet, tamper-seal orange; sealed-ballot hero, nine-seal process chain, returns-sheet comparison, incident reports.
pieces.brief:
Election Logistics (more clever title needed)
Pegged to the US elections coming up next week, create an interactive HTML guide exploring the hidden logistics behind elections worldwide, from voter registration and ballot printing to polling-place operations, ballot transport, counting, recounts, and certification.
Explain how election systems differ across countries, including paper ballots, electronic voting, mail voting, voter identification, and proportional versus winner-take-all systems.
Use the US as the main case study but include other countries with key places in the world power structure.
Investigate the people, physical infrastructure, security procedures, deadlines, and logistical failure points required to turn millions of individual votes into certified results.
Include surprising real-world examples of election logistics succeeding, failing, or being challenged, clearly distinguishing documented facts from allegations.
Build an interactive election-process flowchart and country comparison tool that reveals how votes move from voter to final result.
Use original HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and SVG; no external images or copyrighted visual assets.

pieces.title: Six Lost Beers, Brewed Again
pieces.dek: Six regional beers that faded or vanished, what the evidence says about each, and a starting recipe for every one at homebrew scale, with one written out in full for brew day.
pieces.design: Young Serif, Alegreya, Azeret Mono; quadrille-paper green-grey, iron ink, hydrometer red, SRM beer colours; glass-flight hero, hydrometer strips, documented/modern ledger.
pieces.brief:
The Lost Beer Styles Brewing Notebook
Research question: Which historical regional beers can a modern homebrewer realistically recreate using available ingredients?
Rather than collecting beer recipes indiscriminately, select styles with a documented regional identity and a clear reason to brew them.
Proposed contents
- Six styles, such as Kentucky Common, German Lichtenhainer, French bière de garde, Polish grodziskie, Scandinavian farmhouse ale, and a historically grounded London porter.
- Origins, historical period, and the evidence behind each reconstruction.
- Traditional ingredients versus modern substitutes.
- A practical recipe scaled to a five-gallon batch.
- Estimated original gravity, bitterness, fermentation temperature, and expected flavor.
- A sourcing list for specialty malt, hops, and yeast.
Visual element: A regional map of beer traditions with expandable recipe cards and a timeline.
Sources to start with: Brewers Association Beer Style Guidelines, Historical Beer: An Overview, and brewing-history resources from established brewing organizations. The Brewers Association's current guidelines include a dedicated historical beer category, while also recognizing that modern commercial examples don't always replicate historical beers exactly. 
Finish line: Six concise style profiles and one complete recipe ready for a future brew day. Clearly distinguish documented historical ingredients from modern reconstruction choices.

pieces.title: The Everyday Infrastructure Atlas
pieces.dek: Thirty ferries, funiculars, trams, walkways, stations and markets that make 24 places easier to live in, with what each one solves, how residents use it and how to use it yourself.
pieces.design: Anybody, Petrona, JetBrains Mono; riso newsprint with teal, magenta, yellow overprint; composite city cross-section hero, pictogram key, world/Europe pin maps, numbered plates.
pieces.brief:
The Everyday Infrastructure Atlas
The question: What unusual or overlooked infrastructure makes certain cities especially pleasant to live in, navigate, or explore?
This is the most systems-oriented idea of the five. It looks at the practical mechanisms behind a city's character rather than merely describing its attractions.
What to include
- 30 examples of infrastructure that shapes daily life: ferries, funiculars, coastal trams, integrated rail terminals, public markets linked to transit, and pedestrian connections.
- The city problem each system solves.
- How residents use it, not just tourists.
- A short history and a practical example of using it.
- A comparison of similar systems in different cities.
Interactive element: An atlas filterable by infrastructure type, geography, and everyday function. Selecting a feature reveals a map pin, a short explanation, and an official information link.
Sources to start with: OpenStreetMap, GTFS public-transit data documentation, city transport agencies, and municipal open-data portals. GTFS documentation provides a useful framework for representing stops, routes, and trips in a structured way. 
Finish line: 30 documented examples across at least 10 cities, organized into six infrastructure categories.

pieces.title: The Airport-to-City Reality Index
pieces.dek: Thirty European airports scored on how fast, how often and how late public transport gets you from the terminal to the middle of town, with the scoring rules on show.
pieces.design: Bricolage Grotesque, Spectral; platform-tile grey, navy ink, mode colours (signal red, metro green, tram amber, coach violet); in-carriage strip-map hero, ruled sortable directory.
pieces.brief:
The Airport-to-City Reality Index
The question: Which airports make it easiest to start living like a local immediately after landing, and which quietly consume an hour of your trip?
This connects your interest in airport systems with your preference for efficient travel and avoiding unnecessary driving.
What to include
- 30 airports serving interesting European cities.
- Rail, metro, tram, and bus availability.
- Typical journey time to a central transit hub.
- Number of transfers and whether services run late.
- Whether the airport is actually near the city it claims to serve.
- A separate note for low-cost airports located far outside their advertised destination.
Interactive element: A sortable airport directory with filters for direct rail, journey time, overnight service, and transfer count. A simple scorecard could rate convenience, provided the scoring rules are visible.
Sources to start with: International Air Rail Organisation, Eurostat's airport transport dataset, and official airport and railway websites. The IARO directory is a particularly useful starting point for identifying airport rail links. 
Finish line: 30 airports, comparable access data for each, and a ranked list of the 10 most convenient arrivals.

pieces.title: The Heist File
pieces.dek: Five documented jewel thefts and what courts and investigators established about each, how stolen luxury goods are traced, why video evidence misleads, and a glossary of the trade, for writers who want the public record kept apart from invention.
pieces.design: Instrument Serif, Public Sans, Martian Mono; evidence-kraft with forensic grid, ink and exhibit red; exhibit-tag hero, vertical case-file tabs, CCTV findings panel, verdict timeline.
pieces.brief:
The Anatomy of a Modern Luxury Crime
A writer's reference to the environments, methods, and social machinery behind sophisticated contemporary thefts.
Include: real documented jewel thefts, luxury resale networks, auction houses, private security, identity verification, surveillance evidence, and the distinction between public facts and fictionalized mechanics.
Finish line: five case studies, a glossary of the luxury trade, and a collection of story-generating contradictions. Pay particular attention to mistaken identity and why video evidence can be misleading.
Review: yes

pieces.title: The Cocktail Birthplace Atlas
pieces.dek: Twenty classic cocktails credited to a particular bar, each tested against the earliest printed record, with what stands at the address now and where to order the drink today.
pieces.design: Old Standard TT, Courier Prime, Pinyon Script; birth-register salmon, carmine ruling and stamp-pad inks; guilloche seal, certificate forms with rubber-stamp verdicts, counterfoils, world map with insets.
pieces.brief:
The Cocktail Birthplace Atlas
A companion to The Hotel Bar Atlas: 20 classic cocktails credited to a specific bar, set against what the record supports and what stands at that address today. Many of the famous claims are shakier than the menus suggest. The Negroni's count is disputed, and the Roosevelt's Sazerac Bar bought its name in 1949, so treat every origin as a claim to test.
Include: for each drink, the bar and city credited, the claimed creator and year, the earliest printed recipe or reference found, any rival claimants, how the first known spec differs from what's poured now, and what occupies the original site.
Include: a verdict on a visible four-step scale (documented, credited, contested, legend), defined in the piece, and a status for the room: same room still pouring; moved or rebuilt; a namesake that took the name later; members only; or gone, with what replaced it.
Include: where the drink can still be ordered at or near its birthplace, a short register in the Hotel Bar Atlas manner: getting in, today's price of the drink checked on the day, best time to go, and whether there's a counter for one.
Include: spread across at least eight countries and from the 1850s to the 2000s, with at least three modern classics. Candidates to weigh, not a fixed list: Sazerac, Ramos Gin Fizz and Hurricane (New Orleans), Negroni (Florence), Bellini (Venice), Boulevardier (Paris), Piña Colada (San Juan, two rival claims), Pisco Sour (Lima), Irish Coffee (Foynes and San Francisco), Mai Tai (Oakland), Painkiller (Jost Van Dyke), Caesar (Calgary), Jungle Bird (Kuala Lumpur), Penicillin (New York), Gin Basil Smash (Hamburg), Espresso Martini (London).
Include: a short "too many fathers" note on famous drinks left out because no single bar can claim them (Martini, Margarita, Manhattan, Old Fashioned), and one cautionary tale of an origin story its author later admitted inventing (the Seelbach).
Avoid: re-profiling the five drinks The Hotel Bar Atlas already covers (Singapore Sling at the Long Bar, Vieux Carré at the Monteleone, Red Snapper at the King Cole Bar, Hanky Panky at the American Bar, Serendipity at Bar Hemingway). Link to that piece and keep them out of the 20. Don't print a bar's own story as fact, and don't call any recipe "the original" unless a period source gives it.
Look: a register of births, each drink a certificate with its verdict stamped on it, plus a world map of birthplaces.
Finish line: 20 certificates, a map, a tally of verdicts, and a one-paragraph method for judging any origin claim you meet on a menu.

pieces.title: The Airport Systems Atlas
pieces.dek: How hubs, alliances, transfer rules, borders and airport rail links shape a journey, with five worked trips that judge a route by its door-to-door time and full cost rather than its headline fare.
pieces.design: Barlow Condensed, Atkinson Hyperlegible, Red Hat Mono; wayfinding yellow, terminal-floor grey, ink and exit green; gate-letter sign headers, hub diagram, door-to-door timeline bars.
pieces.brief:
The Airport Systems Atlas
A guide to why airports work the way they do, how they connect to cities, and how travelers can make smarter routing decisions.
Include: hub structures, airline alliances, rail-air connections, terminal transfers, overnight connections, ground transport, alternative airports, and examples of counterintuitive routes.
Finish line: five worked journeys showing how to compare total travel time, transfers, ground access, and cost—not merely the headline airfare.

pieces.title: Landfall
pieces.dek: How ten countries physically plug into the internet: the cables, exchanges and satellites they rely on, where those links run thin, and what three real outages did to ordinary people.
pieces.design: Big Shoulders Display, Literata, IBM Plex Mono; cable-jacket grey, graphite, copper and twelve fibre-code colours; cable cross-section hero, schematic route map, fault-ticket case files.
pieces.brief:
The Invisible Systems That Keep Countries Connected
Explore the physical and commercial infrastructure behind the digital world: submarine cables, internet exchanges, mobile operators, satellite systems, and international data routes.
Include: 10 strategically interesting countries, major infrastructure, operators, dependencies, chokepoints, redundancy, and geopolitical implications.
Finish line: a sourced explainer with a map or network diagram and three case studies of how disruptions can affect ordinary users.

pieces.title: The Clock Gap
pieces.dek: Twenty places where a government set the clocks on purpose and wrote down why, from Franco's Spain to Pyongyang's half-hour, with a live board showing how far each one runs from the sun.
pieces.design: Gloock, Source Serif 4, Spline Sans Mono; enamel blue-white, ink, vermilion, time-ball yellow; UTC offset band hero, sun-gap rulers, dark live board.
pieces.brief:
The Clock Gap
A field guide to time zones as political decisions: Spain on Central European Time since 1940, Nepal’s +5:45 offset, China’s single zone, North Korea’s 2015–18 “Pyongyang time.”
Rule: only offsets that a government chose for a documented reason.
Finish: 20 entries plus a live offset widget.
Why now: Europe falls back Oct 25 and the US on Nov 1, so New York–London runs four hours apart for a week. This extends Deadline Clock, so publish it first.

pieces.title: Where Quiet Money Settled
pieces.dek: Ten European villa districts and resort enclaves, from Cascais to Saltsjöbaden, and the land companies, railways and building rules that made them look the way they do.
pieces.design: Libre Caslon Display/Text with Archivo Narrow; survey-linen, Prussian blue and surveyor's red; subdivision-plat hero, graticule map, deed-clause register boxes.
pieces.brief:
The Secret Geography of European Luxury
Investigate where understated wealth actually lives: villa districts, seaside enclaves, resort towns, and overlooked neighborhoods with exceptional architecture and views.
Include: 10 locations, property styles, local wealth indicators, architectural history, nearby amenities, transport access, and representative properties or streets.
Finish line: a visual atlas that explains why each place feels distinctive. Use public property listings and documented examples rather than speculating about private residents or their finances.

pieces.title: The Hotel Bar Atlas
pieces.dek: Twenty hotel bars around the world where anyone can walk in, take a seat and watch a city, sorted by the kind of evening they offer.
pieces.design: Bodoni Moda, Newsreader and Jost; letterhead cream, claret and bottle green with brass; key-rack index, lobby clocks, ledger-style register cards.
pieces.brief:
The Hotel Bar Atlas
A guide to hotel bars as urban third places: where you can sit comfortably, observe a city, meet people, and enjoy a sense of occasion without staying at the hotel.
Include: 20 bars in cities around the world, architectural identity, neighborhood context, price expectations, solo-visitor friendliness, best time to visit, and public access policies.
Finish line: a curated directory organized by atmosphere, not just by star rating. Favor places that offer a window into their city over generic luxury interiors.
